analysis.one_liner: A friend tried calling me today, which is already unsettling, but her voice sounded off.
analysis.headline: I keep worrying that something's wrong with her, but I can't figure out what.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill, S. 1680, creates procedures for challenging NSLs in court and adds new penalty provisions.
analysis.who_benefits: Recipients of NSLs, such as telecoms, credit bureaus, and banks, would gain the ability to petition courts to modify or block overbroad demands for customer records, and to challenge the attached gag orders that currently bar them from ever telling anyone the FBI came asking.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Telecom, credit, and bank record holders

how_it_helps.text: Recipients of NSLs could petition a U.S. district court to modify or set aside the request itself if compliance would be unreasonable or oppressive.

The bill sets up a process for challenging the nondisclosure requirement: within one year, a court could lift the gag unless disclosure would endanger national security, interfere with an investigation, or endanger life; after a year, the issuing officer must either lift it or recertify, and recertifications are treated as conclusive unless made in bad faith.
Court proceedings challenging NSLs would be closed and kept under seal to prevent unauthorized disclosure of the requests.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the FBI and other intelligence agencies would lose some of the unilateral ability to compel records without any judicial check, and would bear the cost of defending challenges in court.
analysis.who_pays_short: FBI and intelligence agencies' unchecked record access

drawbacks.text: The judicial check was narrow: the government's certification that disclosure may endanger national security or diplomatic relations would be treated as conclusive unless a court found it was made in bad faith, and a denied petition would bar the recipient from refiling for a year.

The bill actually strengthened secrecy in one respect: it wrote new criminal penalties (up to one year, or five if intended to obstruct an investigation) for violating the nondisclosure rules that prohibit recipients from telling anyone the FBI sought their records.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give businesses that receive NSLs their only real avenue to push back in court, but the checks were modest — certifications are presumed valid, and the bill adds new criminal penalties reinforcing the gag regime rather than dismantling it.

outcome.mechanism: Cornyn introduced it in September 2005; it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 12, 2005, and read twice before being referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.
No further action was recorded after the referral; it never advanced through committee or reached the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The FBI and other agencies retained the ability to issue NSLs with no judicial review of the requests or the attached gag orders, and telecom, credit, and financial companies continued to face the choice of complying silently or facing legal consequences for disclosure.

for.name: Sen. John Cornyn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the floor.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chair Arlen Specter
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action on the bill for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew no cosponsors and no recorded floor opposition; with no votes or committee activity, no party-line pattern is visible.

industries.note: These companies are the ones served with NSLs for phone and internet records; the bill would have let them challenge overbroad demands and gag orders in court, but also expanded the confidentiality rules they must enforce and added criminal penalties for violating them.

Banks and consumer reporting agencies receive NSLs for financial and credit records; the bill would have created a judicial pathway for them to contest the demands, while adding new statutory confidentiality obligations and penalties.
